title: You are the man (2 Samuel 12:1–13)
hookLine: Nathan tells a story about a poor man's lamb, and David convicts himself
carry: I have sinned against the Lord

lines: A SON IS BORN. NO ONE SPEAKS.
cards: Uriah is dead. Bathsheba lives in David's house. A son is born.
The text records no one saying a word to the king. Then the prophet Nathan comes, sent by God. He doesn't accuse anyone.
He asks the king for a ruling on a case. Two men in one city, he says, one rich and one poor. The rich man had flocks and herds, a great many.
The poor man had nothing but one little ewe lamb. And David, who was a shepherd before he was a king, leans in to listen.

teach.b: Nathan describes that lamb, in the King James Bible: it "grew up together with him, and with his children; it did eat of his own meat, and drank of his own cup, and lay in his bosom, and was unto him as a daughter."
A pet. Family. Then a traveler visits the rich man, who doesn't want to take from his own flock, so he takes the poor man's lamb and serves it for dinner.
David explodes: "As the LORD liveth, the man that hath done this thing shall surely die." The lamb must be repaid fourfold, because the man had no pity. He has pronounced the sentence.
And Nathan says it: "Thou art the man." The story was a mirror, and David walked right up to it.
Nathan goes on in God's name: I anointed you, I gave you everything, and if that had been too little I would have given you more. Why did you despise the commandment?
You killed Uriah with the sword of the Ammonites, and took his wife. A king could have had him thrown out. David doesn't.

teach.h: I HAVE SINNED AGAINST THE LORD.
teach.b: He says: "I have sinned against the LORD." No excuse. No list of reasons.
Nathan answers at once: "The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die." Forgiven, though the chapter goes on to say there will still be consequences.
The heading of Psalm fifty-one ties that psalm to this very moment, when Nathan came to David, and some Christians pray it as a prayer of repentance.

how: Some Christians read Nathan's rebuke together with Psalm 51, whose heading links it to this moment, and some pray Psalm 51 as a prayer of confession.

o: the king's scribe who wrote down the psalms
the prophet who told David, thou art the man
the priest who raised Samuel at Shiloh

s: Nathan accused David directly from the start
he told a story and asked the king to judge it first.
David passed sentence on himself without knowing it
he said the rich man deserved to die, and Nathan said: thou art the man.
David made excuses when he was confronted
he said: "I have sinned against the LORD."

games.q: you're David. a prophet has just told you that the cruel rich man in his story is you. what do you say?
o: explain why it wasn't really like that.
I have sinned against the LORD.
games.why: "I have sinned against the LORD." and Nathan answers at once that the LORD has put away his sin.

practice: Think of the last time someone told you something true about yourself that you didn't want to hear, and go back to it slowly with one question: was any of it true?
If some of it was, don't defend yourself in your head; just let it stand there, like Nathan in the doorway. If you pray, you can bring it before God in silence.

wordCard.voice: Nathan. The prophet who told David a story about a rich man and a poor man's lamb, until the king realized he was the guilty judge.
